title: Don Quixote
synopsis: La Mancha. You read too many books and got the wrong ideas. Today you put on a rusted helmet and call your old horse Rocinante. You will be, you have decided, a knight.

nodes.text: Four hundred books, floor to beam, and the middle shelf bowing like an old horse's back. You have read them all twice, and the second reading is the one that did the damage. Outside, a hen is conducting business in the yard. Inside, a knight is getting out of a chair very slowly, at fifty.

choices.consequence: You promise the books a bonfire the way a man promises to quit tomorrow. Then you pack four of them in a sack for the road.
You load six volumes onto a horse who is already a standing argument against carrying anything. He looks back at you exactly once.

nodes.text: You build the visor out of card and glue, then test it with one blow of the sword. It comes apart immediately, which is data. You rebuild it and do not test it again, which is philosophy. A barber's basin completes the arrangement. Your housekeeper watches the whole procedure from the doorway and says nothing she will later admit to.

choices.consequence: You cross the yard with your chin up and the basin catching the sun. Two farmhands stop working entirely to watch you go.
You carry it under one arm until the road bends out of sight of the village, then put it on. Nobody is fooled. Nobody is watching.

nodes.text: He is twenty-one years old, mostly hip bone, and has spent his life pulling a cart in a straight line. You spend four days choosing his name, which is longer than you spent choosing your own. When you say it aloud he does not react. When you climb on, he simply starts walking. It's the willingness that undoes you.

choices.consequence: You tell him he is the finest steed in Spain. He is not. He is the only creature alive who has never questioned the plan.
You touch your heels to his ribs and he goes from slow to slightly less slow. You call it a gallop. History will call it otherwise.

nodes.text: Sancho Panza has four children, one donkey, and no talent whatsoever for saying no. You offer him an island to govern. He asks how big. You say very. He asks his wife, who tells him he's a fool; he agrees with her, packs bread and a wineskin, and is at your gate before dawn.

choices.consequence: You swear on your sword he'll have an island and a hat to go with it. He asks about the hat for the next two hundred miles.
You admit the island is theoretical. Sancho chews that over a while, then says a theoretical island still beats a real field in August.

nodes.text: Thirty of them on the plain, arms turning in a wind coming off the wheat. Giants, obviously: the arms, the height, the arrogance of just standing there. Sancho says the word 'windmills' four times, each time slower than the last. You lower the lance. Rocinante, to his eternal credit, does not raise a single objection.

choices.consequence: You cover two hundred yards at the speed of an elderly cart horse, which turns out to be enough. The sail takes the lance, then takes you.
You pull up short and study the nearest giant for a long moment. It keeps turning. Not stopping, you conclude, is exactly what a giant would do.

nodes.text: You come down with the lance in three pieces and one rib doing something new. Sancho gets under your arm and hauls you upright, complaining without pause, and does not once say the thing he has every right to say. The mill keeps turning behind you. It has no opinion at all. That's the worst of it.

choices.consequence: You explain that an envious enchanter turned them into mills at the final instant. Sancho nods along and quietly repositions your shoulder.
You say the word out loud, once, into the dirt. Sancho pretends not to have heard, which is the kindest act performed all month.

nodes.text: The inn has a pig in the yard and a roof with opinions. You call it a castle, address the innkeeper as its lord, and request the order of knighthood before morning. He looks at the two mule drivers by the fire, then back at you, then decides — you can watch him decide — that this will be cheaper than arguing.

choices.consequence: You kneel two hours on flagstones guarding your armor beside a horse trough. A mule driver tries to move it and learns something about you.
You pay in advance for a ceremony he invents on the spot out of a ledger book and a stable boy's laughing. Worth every coin.

nodes.text: Eleven goatherds, one fire, an unreasonable quantity of cheese. You stand and deliver forty minutes on the Golden Age, when the earth gave freely and no man said the word 'mine.' They hear you all the way to the end. One of them, afterward, offers you more cheese. It is the only review you will ever receive and you take it as a rave.

choices.consequence: You continue another twenty minutes into a second speech concerning acorns. Two goatherds fall asleep sitting up. Sancho eats their share of supper.
You sit down mid-thought and pass the wineskin along. The oldest goatherd immediately starts a far better story about a girl and a dead shepherd.

nodes.text: Twelve men chained at the neck, walking toward the oars for the rest of their lives. You interview each one, find the reasoning of the state unpersuasive, and take on six guards to cut them loose. Then you ask the twelve to travel to El Toboso and present themselves to a lady. They look at you. Then they stone you and scatter.

choices.consequence: You sit down in the road and count the stones they left behind. Sancho points out, gently, that the guards are coming back with friends.
Bleeding from one ear, you argue that freeing a man is right regardless of what he does with the freedom. Sancho doesn't disagree. He just walks faster.

nodes.text: He lives up in the rocks above the goat paths, barefoot, beard to his chest. He'll talk for an hour perfectly sensibly, then hit one particular name and go off like a dropped pot. His story has a friend in it, and a wedding, and a letter that arrived late. You have never in your life met anyone more like you.

choices.consequence: You let him reach the end without correcting the chronology once. Afterward he sleeps eleven hours straight. Sancho sits and watches him breathe.
You interrupt to explain what a knight would have done about the wedding. He throws a rock at you. It is, in fairness, a fair rock.

nodes.text: Her name is Aldonza Lorenzo. She salts pork better than anyone in the district and has a voice that carries four fields. You have seen her, perhaps, twice. In your accounting she is Dulcinea del Toboso, of unrivalled beauty, whose hair is gold — you have committed publicly to gold — and who has never been informed of any of this.

choices.consequence: You hold the belief the way a man holds a door for a queen who isn't coming. It costs you nothing, and also everything.

choices.text: Send her a letter signed your knight
choices.consequence: You dictate three pages to Sancho, who cannot write, and send him off with it memorized. He loses the middle page somewhere near a tavern.

nodes.text: A barber rides past in the rain with his brass basin on his head to keep dry. You relieve him of it at lance-point and he runs, sensibly, leaving behind the basin, the mule, and his dignity in that order. There's a semicircular notch cut in it for a throat. You explain the helmet was damaged in a legendary battle. Sancho says nothing for a mile.

choices.consequence: You wear it, and rain collects in the notch and runs down inside your collar for six hours. You do not mention this to anyone.
You leave it on a stone by the road with two coins inside it. The barber, watching from behind a wall, waits until you're small on the horizon.

nodes.text: He does the arithmetic out loud on a Tuesday: months served, meals missed, one donkey stolen and recovered, a blanket, six teeth loosened at various inns. He never raises his voice. He has clearly been assembling this figure for weeks. The figure is entirely fair. You have, in actual coin, roughly one ninth of it.

choices.consequence: You upgrade the island to an island with a harbour. He accepts it. You both know precisely what has occurred and neither of you says so.
You sell the good saddle and count the coins into his hand in daylight. He gives two back for supper, and the account is closed.

nodes.text: They have read about you. That is the entire joke, and it takes you a week not to get it. They give you a room with tapestries, they call you 'your grace,' they arrange an enchanted wooden horse and hire nine servants to be amazed by it. For the first time in your life you are treated exactly as you have always insisted you should be.

choices.consequence: You thank them in formal Castilian for a hospitality that is a joke at your expense. The duchess, briefly, stops laughing.
Something at the corner of the duke's mouth catches you. You let it pass. Suspecting would cost more than the tapestries are worth.

nodes.text: They hand him a town of a thousand souls purely to watch a farmer fail at it. He governs ten days. He settles a debt case by weighing a walking stick, cuts the price of shoes, refuses every bribe including one very good one, and eats almost nothing because his doctor keeps removing the plates. Then he hands the town back.

choices.consequence: You tell him he governed better than most kings. He shrugs and says he only asked people what happened, then believed the quieter one.
For one ugly hour you resent a farmer for being good at the thing you promised him. Then comes the shame, which lasts considerably longer.

nodes.text: They lower you sixty feet on a rope and haul you out an hour later, asleep. Down there, you report, was a crystal palace, three centuries of enchanted knights, and a lady who sent a servant up to borrow six coins, because even the enchanted have expenses. Sancho asks a follow-up question about the coins. You have no answer prepared.

choices.consequence: You add that you cannot swear whether you slept. It's the most honest sentence of your entire knighthood and not one person present notices.
By supper the palace has acquired a second courtyard and a river. Sancho, who lies professionally, watches you work and looks almost proud.

nodes.text: He rides onto the beach at Barcelona in white armor with a moon on the shield and challenges you properly, in form, with witnesses. His terms: if you lose, you go home and hang up the lance for a full year. You know that voice. You have known that voice since you were nine. The terms are honourable. The voice is a neighbour's.

choices.consequence: You agree to his terms in front of forty people on wet sand. Sancho tries to catch your eye and you refuse, deliberately, to give it.
You cite a technicality concerning the challenger's blazon. Everyone lets you have it, which is worse than losing and takes about eleven seconds.

nodes.text: It takes roughly four seconds. He comes in level, you go off backwards, and the sand is harder than sand has any business being. From under the visor you tell him he may kill you but that Dulcinea remains the most beautiful woman alive. He says he'd honestly rather you just went home. You ride out of Barcelona at a walk, in the rain.

choices.consequence: You say nothing for two days. Sancho fills the silence with an extremely long story about a goat, entirely for your benefit.
You outline a rematch schedule, a training regime, and an improvement to the shield. Sancho agrees with every word and steers the donkey homeward.

nodes.text: You go to bed on a Thursday and stay there. The priest comes, then the barber, then the priest again. Your niece changes the linen and tells you it's the fall and the rain that did it, not the books. Sancho sits at the foot of the bed with his hat in both hands, weeping, proposing that the two of you become shepherds instead.

choices.consequence: You ask for the notary and a clean shirt. Your niece leaves the room to do her crying where the arithmetic of it won't show.
You and Sancho name six sheep you do not own and never will. He plays along at full volume. It is his last and best service.

nodes.text: You sit up clear-eyed for the first time in a week, say your own name — the real one, the one on the land deed — and renounce every romance you ever read. The priest writes it down carefully. Sancho, from the corner, commits the plainest heresy in the room: get up, we'll go out again, the giants are still there.

choices.consequence: You mean every word, and the room relaxes, and something in Sancho's face goes out like a lamp carried into another part of the house.
You renounce the books in a voice that leaves one door unlatched. The priest hears it. He writes down the other version regardless.

nodes.text: It takes three days and is, by the standards of the age, comfortable. There's a will, a notary, and a clause forbidding your niece to marry any man who reads adventures. Afterward the village is quieter in a way that is not restful. Sancho stands in the yard holding a donkey's rope, unable to think what to do with his hands.

choices.consequence: You go out with your mouth doing something the priest records as peace and your niece records, privately, as the old nonsense to the end.
One tear, badly timed, on the word 'squire.' Sancho hears it from the corridor and has to go outside and stand by the well.
You say one last sentence too quietly for anyone in the room to catch, and the village spends thirty years arguing about what it was.

nodes.text: The priest and the barber go along the shelves sentencing books like a court in session. Most burn in the yard; four are pardoned on literary merit and one because the barber liked the cover. The village reads the survivors aloud on winter nights — first with skepticism, then with less, then with a man doing all the voices. Nobody in La Mancha burns anything after that.

Sancho tells it at the inn to whoever will hold still, and the story improves in his mouth the way bread improves in an oven. The windmills grow taller. The lance acquires a name. Within a generation the children along that road know a version in which the giants were real, and they are not wrong, and Sancho — who was actually there — never once corrects them.

A one-handed veteran with debts and a good ear writes you down. He gets the donkey wrong and the bruises exactly right. The book outlives every kingdom you meant to conquer, gets translated forty times, and turns your name into an adjective that people use slightly incorrectly forever. You set out to be a knight. You became a joke four centuries have failed to wear out.
